subject: Geography
board: National Curriculum (KS1-3), aligned to AQA GCSE 9-1
source: National Curriculum (KS1 geography: continents and oceans, hot and cold places, atlas and compass skills)

lessons.title: The seven continents
objectives: Find each continent on a world map or globe
Say which continent is the biggest

keywords.def: one of the seven very large areas of land on Earth
a ball-shaped model of the Earth
a flat picture of the whole Earth

starter: Say Bismillah. Name the four countries of the UK.
What do we call a drawing of a place from above?
What is the name of the country where we live?

teach.heading: Our big planet
bullets: We live on planet Earth.
Earth has land and water.
The big areas of land are called continents.
teach.note: Hold up a globe or show one on screen and turn it slowly. Ask: what colours can you see? Blue is water and other colours are land. Say that Allah created the Earth with land and sea. Explain that a continent is a very big piece of land, much larger than a country.

teach.heading: Seven continents
bullets: Asia, Africa, North America and South America.
Antarctica, Europe and Australia.
There are seven continents in all.
teach.note: Use a chant to learn the names: tap out the number of seven on your fingers. Show each continent in a different colour. Some maps show Australia as Oceania - say both names. Misconception: children think the UK is a continent. Remind them that the UK is a country in the continent of Europe.

teach.heading: Biggest and smallest
bullets: Asia is the biggest continent.
Australia is the smallest continent.
Antarctica is covered in ice.
teach.note: Compare sizes by showing the continents as coloured shapes on a screen. Ask: which is bigger, Africa or Europe? Africa is much bigger. Link to home: many families have roots in Asia or Africa; ask children to point out where their family comes from.

teach.heading: Where are we?
bullets: The UK is in the continent of Europe.
Makkah is in Asia, in the country of Saudi Arabia.
Egypt is in the north of Africa.
teach.note: Point to each place on the map. Ask children to name a place they have visited and say which continent it is in. Makkah is a place Muslims all over the world face when they pray; this helps children connect the map with their own lives.

practice: On the world map, point to Asia, Africa and Europe as I say them.
Complete: 'The UK is in the continent of ___.'
independent: Colour in the seven continents on the world map and write their names.
Label the continent where you live and the continent where your family comes from.
Stretch: put the continents in order from biggest to smallest using a table.
exit: Which continent is the UK in?
lessons.homework: Find the seven continents on a globe or map at home and teach someone how to say them.
lessons.send: Provide a map with the continents outlined and name cards to stick on. EAL: say each continent name together twice. Stretch: ask which continents the Equator crosses.

lessons.title: The five oceans
objectives: Find the oceans on a world map
Say that most of the Earth is covered by water

keywords.def: a very large area of salt water
the ocean between Europe/Africa and the Americas
a smaller part of an ocean, often near land

starter: Which continent is the UK in?

teach.heading: Water on Earth
bullets: Most of the Earth is covered by water.
About 7 out of every 10 parts is water.
The biggest areas of water are oceans.
teach.note: Show a globe from the Pacific side so that nearly all you see is blue. Ask: is there more land or more water? Say 'about seven parts out of ten are water'. Use a picture of 10 squares with 7 coloured blue if helpful.

teach.heading: Five oceans
bullets: Pacific, Atlantic, Indian, Southern and Arctic.
The Pacific Ocean is the biggest.
The Arctic Ocean is the smallest.
teach.note: Teach the names with a rhythm: Pa-ci-fic, At-lan-tic. Colour each ocean on the map in a different shade of blue. Ask children to point to the ocean that touches the UK: the Atlantic (and the North Sea, which is part of it).

teach.heading: Oceans and continents
bullets: Oceans lie between the continents.
The Atlantic lies between Europe and America.
The Indian Ocean is next to Africa and Asia.
teach.note: Move your finger along the coasts. Ask: if you sailed west from the UK across the Atlantic, which continent would you reach? (North America). Keep language simple and use arrows on the map.

teach.heading: Looking after the sea
bullets: Many animals live in the ocean.
Litter and plastic can harm sea animals.
We can reuse, recycle and put litter in the bin.
teach.note: Show a picture of a turtle or fish tangled in plastic. Ask children how it must feel. Connect to being kind to Allah's creation and looking after the Earth as a trust. Ask them to suggest one thing they can do at home.

practice: Point to the Pacific Ocean and the Atlantic Ocean on the map.
Say: 'The Indian Ocean is next to ___.' Choose a continent.
independent: Label the five oceans on a world map.
Colour the oceans in blue and the continents in green.
Stretch: write one sentence about an animal that lives in the ocean.
exit: Is there more land or more water on Earth?
lessons.homework: Draw an ocean animal and write the name of the ocean where it lives.
lessons.send: Use pre-labelled oceans for support. EAL: rehearse ocean names with a rhythm. Stretch: ask which ocean is nearest to the child's family home country.

lessons.title: Hot and cold places: the Equator and the Poles
objectives: Find the Equator, the North Pole and the South Pole
Say that places near the Equator are hot and places near the Poles are cold
Describe one hot place and one cold place

keywords.def: an imaginary line around the middle of the Earth
the very top of the Earth, a very cold place
the very bottom of the Earth, a very cold place
a place that gets very little rain

starter: Is it hot or cold outside today in the UK?

teach.heading: The Equator
bullets: The Equator is an imaginary line.
It goes around the middle of the Earth.
It is not a real line on the ground.
teach.note: Use a globe or a ball with a string around the middle. Point to countries that the Equator crosses, such as Ecuador, Kenya and Indonesia. Misconception: some pupils think the Equator is a real line you can see. Explain that it is a line drawn on maps to help us.

teach.heading: Hot places
bullets: Places near the Equator are hot.
The sun shines strongly there all year.
The Sahara in Africa is a very hot desert.
teach.note: Show a photograph of the Sahara and of a hot rainforest. Ask: what do people wear? What do plants and animals need to survive? Explain that a desert gets very little rain but a rainforest gets lots of rain, and both can be hot.

teach.heading: Cold places
bullets: The North Pole is at the top of the Earth.
The South Pole is at the bottom.
Places near the Poles are very, very cold.
teach.note: Show Antarctica and the Arctic on the globe. Share that in Antarctica the temperature has fallen to about minus 89 degrees Celsius, the coldest ever recorded. Ask: what clothes would you need? Explain that polar bears live in the Arctic and penguins in Antarctica.

teach.heading: Where is the UK?
bullets: The UK is between the Equator and the North Pole.
The UK is not very hot or very cold.
We have mild weather with four seasons.
teach.note: Use a sorting line: hot (Equator), medium (UK), cold (Pole). Ask where the UK sits and why we need both coats and sun hats in a year. Praise children for using 'because'.

practice: Point to the Equator on the globe. Point to the North Pole.
Sort the pictures into hot places and cold places.
independent: Draw the Equator and the two Poles on a picture of the Earth.
Colour the hot places red and the cold places blue.
Stretch: write two sentences comparing a hot place and a cold place.
exit: Are places near the Equator hot or cold?
lessons.homework: Draw what you would pack for a trip to the Sahara and what you would pack for the North Pole.
lessons.send: Give a labelled globe diagram. EAL: pair words with pictures (hot/cold, near/far). Stretch: ask why it is warmer near the Equator, using the idea that the sun shines more directly.

lessons.title: Using an atlas and a compass
objectives: Use an atlas or world map to find a place
Use north, south, east and west to describe where places are

keywords.def: the direction towards the North Pole
which way something is, like north or south

starter: Say Bismillah. Is the Equator hot or cold?
Which continent is the UK in?

teach.heading: What is an atlas?
bullets: An atlas is a book of maps.
It shows continents, countries and cities.
There is an index at the back to find places.
teach.note: Show an atlas or an online atlas page. Model looking up Egypt in the index and finding the page. Ask children how the index is like the contents page of a story book. Keep a copy of the world map visible throughout.

teach.heading: Four compass points
bullets: The four main directions are north, east, south and west.
North is usually at the top of a map.
Never Eat Soggy Waffles helps us remember the order.
teach.note: Draw a compass rose and label N, E, S, W going clockwise. Teach the rhyme 'Never Eat Shredded Wheat' or 'Never Eat Soggy Waffles'. Have children stand and point north (the front of the room), then east to their right. Muslims also use direction when finding the qibla: it is the direction of the Kaaba in Makkah.

teach.heading: Describing where places are
bullets: Scotland is north of England.
Wales is west of England.
France is south of the UK.
teach.note: Use a map of the UK and Europe. Ask children to complete sentences: ___ is north of ___. Watch for children confusing east and west. Point out that on a map, east is to the right.

teach.heading: Finding a place
bullets: Choose a place and find it in the index.
Turn to the page and find the place.
Say which continent and direction it is.
teach.note: Model three steps aloud (think aloud). Example: find Egypt. The index gives a page. On the map, Egypt is in the north of Africa and south-east of the UK. Give children a place card each to find on their own map.

practice: Use the compass rose to say which direction Scotland is from England.
Find Egypt on the map and say which continent it is in.
independent: Label the compass rose with N, E, S and W.
Complete five sentences using north, south, east and west about places on the UK map.
Stretch: write directions to move from the school gate to the library on a simple map.
exit: What do we call a book of maps?
Which direction is at the top of most maps?
lessons.homework: Use a map or phone compass to find north in your home and tell someone which room is in the north.
lessons.send: Provide a compass rose with the letters partly filled in. EAL: practise direction words with movement. Stretch: introduce north-east and north-west.
